なんじ です か — What time is it?
You tell the time, talk about your day with verbs in the ～ます form (I get up, I work, I go to bed) and say “from … to …”.
I go to bed, I sleep
I rest, I take a break
I get up at six every morning.
I work from nine to five.
To tell and ask the time: なんじ です か / さんじ はん です.
To use verbs in the polite ～ます form in 4 versions: today/tomorrow, not, yesterday, not yesterday.
To say what time you do something: ろくじ に おきます.
To say “from … to …”: くじ から ごじ まで.
A long day at the hospital
In the evening, Mihai calls Yuki after a long shift at the hospital in Madrid. Yuki wants to know what a doctor’s day is like.
Hello, Mihai? What time is it now?
It’s nine in the evening now. I’ve just finished work.
What, nine?! That’s tough! What time did you start?
I worked from seven in the morning until nine at night.
So what time do you get up every morning?
I get up at half past five. Then at half past six I go to the hospital.
Do you have a lunch break?
Yes, I take a break from one to half past one. But today I didn’t take a break.
No, not yet. I’m going to eat now.
No, tomorrow is my day off! I’m sleeping until ten.
How nice! Then tomorrow let’s study Japanese together.
Yes! At three in the afternoon, at the library. Good night.
Three hours are read irregularly: よじ (4, not “yonji”), しちじ (7), くじ (9, not “kyūji”). Repeat them 5 times.
Minutes change depending on the number: いっぷん (1), さんぷん (3), ごふん (5), じゅっぷん (10). The p has a little pause before it (っ).
“okimasu” sounds like “okimas”, “hatarakimashita” sounds like “hatarakimash’ta”. The i in “shi” is swallowed.
You tell the time like this: NUMBER + じ (ji). “Three o’clock” = さんじ. For minutes add ～ふん/～ぷん, and for “half past” はん.
ごぜん (a.m.) and ごご (p.m.) come BEFORE the time: ごご さんじ = 15:00. More simply, say あさ (in the morning) or よる (in the evening): よる の くじ = 21:00.
2. Verbs in the ～ます form: four versions
The good news: Japanese verbs do NOT change with the person! おきます means “I get up / you get up / he gets up / we get up…”. Context tells you who. You only have 4 endings to learn:
I get up / I will get up
～ます is also used for the future: あした はたらきます = I’m working / I’ll work tomorrow. Japanese has no separate future tense.
Learners often say “はたらきますでした”. Wrong! The past is はたらきました. Only the past negative has でした: はたらきませんでした.
3. At what time? The particle に
For an exact time, put に after it: “at six o’clock” = ろくじ に. The verb comes at the end.
I go to bed at eleven.
With relative time words you DON’T use に: きょう, あした, きのう, まいあさ, いま. Wrong: “あした に はたらきます”. Correct: “あした はたらきます”.
A rule of thumb: if it has a number (a time, a date), use に. If it’s “today / tomorrow / yesterday / every day”, use nothing.
から = from, まで = until / to. They go AFTER the word (like all particles): くじ から = “from nine”.
The lunch break is from one.
They also work with places: マドリード から とうきょう まで = from Madrid to Tokyo.
Now everything combines in a single sentence. Look at how the particles link up:
I study at the library every day from nine.
the place where you do the action
で vs に: で = where you DO something (としょかん で べんきょうします), に = where you ARE / where you go (としょかん に います / いきます).
あした is a relative time word → no に.
What time did Mihai finish work?
ケンジさん の いちにち — Kenji’s day
Kenji, the cook from chapter 2, describes a day at his restaurant.
I’m Kenji. I’m a cook at a restaurant.
Every morning I get up at eight. I drink a coffee.
At ten I go to the market. I buy fish and vegetables.
The restaurant is open from half past eleven until ten at night.
From three to five in the afternoon I take a break. That’s when I have a little sleep.
In the evening, the restaurant is very busy.
Work finishes at eleven. I go to bed at one.
Mondays are my day off. On Mondays I do nothing!
What does Kenji buy at the market?
When does Kenji take a break?

Every day he gets up at half past five. But yesterday his alarm clock didn’t go off.
At eleven he had breakfast. There was bread, eggs and coffee.
Then he went to the park. There were lots of people in the park.
There were dogs and children too. The weather was lovely.
At one in the afternoon he had lunch at Kenji’s place.
“No, it’s my day off! Today I’m doing nothing!”
